p.i: & uiolentiam terra, & ciuitatis, omni-umq; habitantium in ea.

main_text.p: Sunt qui hæc uerba restringant ad po-pulum Iudaicum, à Babylonijs uic[?]tum & abductum in tristissimum exilium: & ad urbem Ierosolymam, quæ ab ijsdem expugnata est, & una cum templo incen-sa & solo æquata, anno mundi 3 3 5 6. ut quidam Chronographi uolunt. Sumitur autem in hac significatione Libani uocabulum, Zach.11.1. Aperi,ô Libane, portas tuas, & absumat ignis cedros tuas. 2.V-lula abies, quia cecidit cedrus, quoniam magnifici uastati sunt: ululate quercus Balan, quoniam deijcietur saltus munitus. Hæc de secunda euersione urbis sanctæ & templi, cuius ὀφγοδιῶκτης diuinitus excitatus, fuit Titus, Vespasiani Imp.F.dici, nemo intelligens dubitare porest.

Certum autem est, Gentes illas, quæ nō tantum in socias & idololatricas gen-tes, sed etiā in Ecclesiam sæuierunt, hu-ius inhumanitatis caussa graviores luere pœnas, eò quòd pupillam oculi Dei, & Christos Domini tetigerunt.
Fatendum tamen est, Libani nomine, κατά

page.notes: The Greek word in the lower right is printed in italic and sits beside the last line, so it is treated as a catchword. Doubtful: "uic[?]tum" (the word after Babylonijs is printed with a ligature that may be "uictum" or similar). The mark over "umq;" in the italic line is uncertain. A small mark beside "gen-" in the right margin looks like a stray glyph and is not transcribed. The Greek word ὀφγοδιῶκτης is copied as it appears on the scan and may be misprinted. The line "Fatendum tamen est, Libani nomine," is followed in the scan by a Greek catchword which may be read as κατά.
